definition: Software that loads Java bytecode and executes it on a particular operating system and CPU.
wrongs: A compiler that turns Java source into a native executable for one operating system.
A source editor that checks syntax before a file is saved.
A library package that stores lists, sets, and maps.
why: Java compiles to bytecode, and the JVM on each host is what actually runs that bytecode.
example: A class file built on a laptop starts correctly on a Linux server that has a compatible runtime.
scenario: A team ships one JAR to Windows servers and Linux laptops. Which component lets that same bytecode run on both?
scenarioWhy: Each machine's JVM executes the same bytecode, so the JAR needs no separate native build per system.

definition: Platform-neutral instructions, stored in class files, that a Java runtime can execute.
wrongs: Native CPU instructions that run only on the machine where they were compiled.
The original Java source kept inside a JAR manifest.
A snapshot of live heap objects taken while a program is paused.
why: javac emits bytecode rather than native machine code so a runtime can execute it on many hosts.
example: Compiling Hello.java produces Hello.class, and a runtime reads those instructions when the program starts.
scenario: After a build, the output folder contains class files but no operating-system executable. What do those class files hold?
scenarioWhy: The compiler writes bytecode into class files, leaving native code generation to the runtime if it happens at all.

definition: The runtime subsystem that finds class files, reads them, and links them before they can be used.
wrongs: A compiler pass that optimizes hot methods into native code.
A collector that frees objects nobody can still reach.
A scheduler that chooses which thread runs next.
why: Classes are brought in on demand, and the class loader is the part that locates and defines them.
example: The first new Student() causes the application loader to read Student.class from the classpath.
scenario: A rarely used feature fails with NoClassDefFoundError only when it is first called. Which runtime part failed to locate that class?
scenarioWhy: The class is loaded when it is first needed, so a missing class file shows up as a class-loader failure at that moment.

definition: Runtime translation of frequently executed bytecode into native machine code.
wrongs: A source compilation that happens only when the file is saved in an editor.
A check that every generic cast is still present at runtime.
A cleanup pass that frees unreachable objects.
why: The runtime watches hot methods and compiles them so later calls can skip interpretation.
example: A loop that ranks a million scores speeds up after the runtime compiles the comparison method.
scenario: A server's first requests are slow, then the same endpoint becomes much faster with no code change. What most likely happened?
scenarioAnswer: Hot methods were compiled at runtime
scenarioWrongs: Packages were merged into one file
scenarioWhy: After methods run often enough, just-in-time compilation turns them into native code for later calls.

definition: Automatic reclamation of heap objects that running code can no longer reach.
wrongs: A compiler warning that deletes unused import declarations.
A manual free call the programmer must make for every object.
A thread scheduler that stops low-priority tasks.
why: The collector traces references from roots and reclaims objects that nothing can still use.
example: After a method drops its only reference to a large byte array, a later collection cycle can reclaim that array.
scenario: A service allocates many short-lived request objects. Which mechanism frees them once no thread can reach them?
scenarioWhy: Unreachable request objects stay on the heap until the collector decides they can be reclaimed.

definition: The runtime memory region where objects and arrays are allocated and shared by threads.
wrongs: The per-thread memory that stores only the currently executing method frames.
The native area that stores class metadata and method bytecode.
The disk folder that stores compiled class files.
why: A new expression reserves object storage on the heap, which all threads of the process can share.
example: Each new Order() created while handling a web request allocates that Order on the shared object area.
scenario: Creating millions of objects throws OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space. Which memory region is exhausted?
scenarioWhy: Objects created with new live on the heap, so exhausting that region raises a heap-space error.

definition: Per-thread memory that holds a frame for each method the thread is currently executing.
wrongs: Shared memory where every object created with new is stored.
Native memory that holds loaded class metadata.
A disk buffer used only for log files.
why: Each call pushes a frame of local variables and a return address, and the frame is popped when the method returns.
example: A recursive factorial method pushes another frame on every call until the base case is reached.
scenario: Deep recursion throws StackOverflowError while plenty of heap space remains. Which memory is exhausted?
scenarioWhy: Each recursive call needs a new frame on that thread's stack, independent of free heap space.

definition: Native memory that stores class metadata such as method information and field layouts.
wrongs: The heap area used only for ordinary object instances.
A per-thread stack of method frames.
A cache of JDBC query results.
why: Since Java 8, class metadata has lived in metaspace instead of a fixed permanent generation on the heap.
example: Generating a new proxy class for every tenant makes native class-metadata memory grow until it hits its limit.
scenario: An app that defines a new class for every tenant eventually fails with Metaspace. What has filled up?
scenarioWhy: Each loaded class adds metadata in metaspace, so unbounded class generation can exhaust that area.

definition: A named namespace that groups related classes and gives them package-private access to one another.
wrongs: A running thread that shares the heap with other threads.
A compiled archive that must contain exactly one class.
A generic type parameter erased at runtime.
why: The package organizes types on the classpath and is the boundary for members with no access modifier.
example: Invoice and Order both live in com.shop.order and can read each other's package-private fields.
scenario: Two classes should share helper methods that outside code must not call, and they should share a namespace. What groups them?
scenarioWhy: Classes in the same package share a namespace and can use each other's package-private members.

definition: A source line that lets code refer to a type by its simple name.
wrongs: A statement that copies another class's bytecode into this file.
A lock that allows only one thread into a method.
A clause that lists checked exceptions a method may throw.
why: The declaration does not load or copy code; it tells the compiler which full type name a short name means.
example: A file that declares import java.util.List can write List instead of java.util.List.
scenario: A source file uses ArrayList with no java.util prefix and still compiles. Which declaration makes that short name legal?
scenarioWhy: An import tells the compiler that the simple name ArrayList means java.util.ArrayList.

definition: A reference type that declares a contract of methods without holding instance fields.
wrongs: A class that stores instance state and can be constructed with new.
A primitive such as int that is not an object.
A package that only groups class files on disk.
why: Implementing classes supply the method bodies, so callers can depend on the contract rather than one class.
example: PaymentGateway requires charge, and both StripeGateway and CashGateway provide their own bodies.
scenario: Unrelated payment classes must all be passable to a method that expects a charge operation. What should they share?
scenarioWhy: An interface lets unrelated classes offer the same methods without sharing one superclass.

definition: A class that cannot be instantiated and may mix concrete methods with unimplemented ones.
wrongs: A final class that can be constructed and has no subclasses.
An interface that is forbidden from containing any method body.
A primitive wrapper that only boxes a single value.
why: Subclasses complete the unimplemented methods, while shared fields and code can live in the abstract superclass.
example: Shape stores a color and a concrete move method, while Circle and Square each implement area.
scenario: Shapes share a color field and a move method, but Shape itself must not be constructed and each shape computes area differently. What should Shape be?
scenarioWhy: An abstract class can hold shared state and code while leaving area for concrete subclasses.

definition: A mechanism that lets a subclass acquire fields and methods from a superclass.
wrongs: A way to pass a block of code as a method argument.
A compiler feature that erases generic type arguments.
A lock that guards a shared field.
why: The extends clause reuses the superclass implementation and lets the subclass add or replace behavior.
example: SavingsAccount extends Account, reuses deposit, and adds its own interest-rate field.
scenario: A new account type should reuse deposit and withdraw instead of copying those methods. Which feature provides that reuse?
scenarioWhy: A subclass inherits the superclass methods, so deposit and withdraw do not need to be copied.

definition: A subclass method with the same signature that replaces the superclass method for subclass objects.
wrongs: Two methods in one class that share a name but take different parameters.
A generic method whose type arguments disappear at runtime.
A static method that hides another static method in a superclass.
why: At a call through a superclass reference, the runtime uses the override belonging to the actual object.
example: Animal declares speak, and a Dog object reached through an Animal variable prints bark from Dog's method.
scenario: A variable of type Animal refers to a Dog, and speak prints bark. Which feature selected Dog's method?
scenarioWhy: The call uses the Dog object's overriding method, not the version declared on the Animal variable.

definition: Several methods in one class that share a name but have different parameter lists.
wrongs: A subclass method that replaces a superclass method with the same parameters.
A method that throws a checked exception to its caller.
A lambda that implements one abstract method.
why: The compiler picks the overload from the argument types at the call site.
example: Printer defines print for a String and print for an int, and the compiler chooses from the argument.
scenario: A utility class has two methods named max, one taking int values and one taking double values. What is that pair?
scenarioWhy: The methods share a name and differ in parameter types, so they are overloads resolved at compile time.

definition: The ability to use different object types through one supertype and still run type-specific behavior.
wrongs: Hiding fields so callers must use methods.
Storing classes in a named namespace.
Reclaiming unreachable objects automatically.
why: A supertype reference may point at any subtype, and overridden methods run the subtype's version.
example: A list of shape references holds circles and squares, and a loop calls area on each reference.
scenario: A checkout method accepts any discount rule, and holiday and student rules compute different amounts. Which idea is in use?
scenarioWhy: One discount-rule type stands for several implementations, and each object applies its own formula.

definition: Hiding an object's data and allowing changes only through its methods.
wrongs: Letting a subclass replace a public method at runtime.
Parameterizing a class with a type argument.
Running two methods at the same time on different threads.
why: Private fields plus public methods keep the object's invariants inside the class.
example: A bank account keeps its balance private and changes it only through deposit and withdraw.
scenario: Callers were setting a balance field negative by writing it directly. Which practice stops that direct write?
scenarioWhy: Keeping the field private forces every change to go through methods that can reject a negative balance.

definition: A way to parameterize classes and methods so the compiler checks the element types.
wrongs: A runtime feature that keeps every type argument available to instanceof.
A keyword that locks a method for one thread.
A stream operation that filters elements.
why: A type such as List of String is rejected at compile time if the code adds the wrong kind of element.
example: A List of String names fails to compile when the code tries to add the integer 42.
scenario: A box type should accept only Invoice objects, and inserting a String should fail at compile time. Which feature does that?
scenarioWhy: A generic box of Invoice lets the compiler reject a String before the program runs.

definition: The compiler's removal of generic type arguments so they are not kept as separate runtime types.
wrongs: A collector pass that deletes unreachable generic objects.
A class-loader step that refuses raw types.
A syntax rule that forbids wildcards in source code.
why: The runtime sees a raw type, and the compiler inserts casts that enforce the generic constraints.
example: At runtime a List of String and a List of Integer are both just List, so a type test for List of String is illegal.
scenario: A method cannot use instanceof to test whether a List is specifically a List of String. Which compilation rule explains that?
scenarioWhy: Generic arguments are erased, so the runtime type of the list does not include String.

definition: A generic parameter restricted to a given type or one of its subtypes.
wrongs: A wildcard that accepts only supertypes of a class.
A raw type with all generic checks turned off.
An array whose length is fixed at compile time.
why: The bound lets the method call operations of the upper bound while still accepting any subtype.
example: A method declared with T extends Number can call doubleValue on every element of a List of T.
scenario: A method must accept a List of Integer or a List of Double and call doubleValue on the elements. How should the type parameter be bounded?
scenarioWhy: An extends Number bound allows Integer and Double and permits calls to Number methods.

definition: A resizable list that stores its elements in a contiguous array.
wrongs: A list of nodes in which each element points to the next element.
A set that rejects duplicates by hashing them.
A map that keeps keys in sorted tree order.
why: Index access jumps directly into the array, and the list copies into a larger array when it is full.
example: A shopping cart stores items so the code can jump straight to item number i.
scenario: A leaderboard needs fast access by position and almost always adds items at the end. Which List implementation fits best?
scenarioWhy: An array-backed list offers constant-time index access and cheap appends until a resize is needed.

definition: A list that stores elements in nodes, each linked to its neighbors.
wrongs: A list that stores elements in one resizable array.
A hash table of unique keys.
A last-in first-out stack of method frames.
why: Inserting or removing at a known node changes a few links instead of shifting an array of elements.
example: A playlist removes the current song by relinking the neighboring songs instead of shifting every later song.
scenario: A queue often inserts and deletes at the ends and almost never looks up an element by index. Which List is a natural fit?
scenarioWhy: Link updates at the ends avoid shifting a contiguous array when the index is rarely needed.

definition: A map from keys to values that places entries in buckets chosen by the key's hash code.
wrongs: A map that always keeps its keys in sorted order.
A list that allows duplicate elements and integer indexes.
A set that stores only true or false.
why: When hash codes spread keys across buckets, get and put take constant time on average.
example: A cache maps each user id to a profile so a lookup does not scan every profile.
scenario: Session data must be retrieved by a unique token in expected constant time. Which collection fits?
scenarioWhy: Hashing the token selects a bucket, so the session can be found without scanning every entry.

definition: A set that rejects duplicate elements by using hash codes and equality.
wrongs: A list that keeps every inserted element, including duplicates.
A map from sorted keys to values.
A queue that removes the oldest element first.
why: Membership tests use hashing, and equals decides whether two objects count as the same element.
example: Adding an email address a second time leaves the set of used addresses unchanged.
scenario: A signup form must remember emails already used and reject a duplicate quickly. Which collection fits?
scenarioWhy: A hash set treats equal emails as one element and tests membership without scanning a list.

definition: A map that keeps its keys in sorted order inside a red-black tree.
wrongs: A map that places keys in hash buckets with no key order.
A set of array indexes with no keys.
A list that sorts only when sort is called.
why: Keys follow Comparable or a Comparator, so iterating the map yields that order.
example: Mapping student names to scores in this structure prints the names in alphabetical order.
scenario: A leaderboard must stay sorted by its score key and still map each key to a player name. Which map fits?
scenarioWhy: A tree map keeps keys ordered, so iteration follows the score order without a separate sort.

definition: An object that visits the elements of a collection one at a time.
wrongs: A compiler that erases generic type arguments.
A lock shared by every thread in a pool.
A cursor over rows returned by a database driver.
why: The iterator hides whether the collection is an array, a linked structure, or a tree, and it can remove the current element safely.
example: A loop walks a task collection and removes a task during the visit when that task is already done.
scenario: Code must visit every element and delete some during the visit without knowing whether the collection is an array or a tree. What should it use?
scenarioWhy: An iterator provides uniform traversal and a remove operation that stays consistent with the collection.

definition: An interface whose compareTo method defines a class's natural order.
wrongs: A separate object that orders two values without changing their class.
A marker interface used only to allow byte-stream output.
A functional interface whose single method is run.
why: Sort methods and tree collections use compareTo when the caller does not supply another ordering.
example: Student implements a natural order by id, so a tree set of students is ordered by that id.
scenario: Student objects should sort by student id inside a tree set, with no extra ordering object. Which interface should Student implement?
scenarioWhy: Comparable puts the natural order inside the class, which a tree set uses automatically.

definition: An object that compares two values using a rule kept outside those values' class.
wrongs: The natural-order method declared inside the class itself.
A hash function that chooses a bucket for a key.
A stream collector that builds a list.
why: An external comparator can order one class in several ways without changing its compareTo method.
example: Products already order themselves by name, while a separate object orders the same products by price.
scenario: Products already sort by name, but one screen must sort those same objects by price. What should that screen pass to the sort?
scenarioWhy: A comparator supplies a price ordering without replacing the class's natural name order.

definition: An object that reports an abnormal condition and can transfer control to a handler.
wrongs: A compile-time warning that never affects control flow.
A second return value stored beside the normal result.
A thread that runs only after the program ends.
why: Throwing the object skips the rest of the normal path and looks for a matching catch.
example: Parsing the text abc as an integer raises NumberFormatException, and a catch turns it into an error message.
scenario: A parser hits bad input and must jump to a handler instead of returning a normal value. What should it throw?
scenarioWhy: Throwing an exception transfers control to a matching handler instead of continuing the normal return path.

definition: An exception that the compiler requires a method to catch or list in its declaration.
wrongs: A RuntimeException that callers may ignore without a compiler error.
An Error that signals a serious failure of the runtime itself.
A warning suppressed with an annotation.
why: Exceptions other than RuntimeException and Error are checked, so they must be handled or declared.
example: Constructing a FileReader can throw FileNotFoundException, so the caller catches it or adds a throws clause.
scenario: The compiler rejects a method that calls a file API and neither catches nor declares the failure. What kind of exception is that?
scenarioWrongs: An error that need not be declared
scenarioWhy: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared, so ignoring a file failure is a compile-time error.

definition: A RuntimeException that callers are not forced to catch or declare.
wrongs: An exception that must appear in a throws clause or a catch.
A checked I/O failure from the file APIs.
An error used only for syntax mistakes.
why: Unchecked exceptions usually report programming bugs such as a bad index or a null reference.
example: Calling get with an index past the end of a list throws IndexOutOfBoundsException with no throws clause required.
scenario: A method may throw ArithmeticException when a computed divisor is zero. What must that method do about the exception?
scenarioAnswer: Nothing special, because it is unchecked
scenarioWrongs: Catch it or add a throws clause
Declare it as a generic bound
scenarioWhy: ArithmeticException is a RuntimeException, so the compiler does not require a catch or a throws clause.

definition: A block that runs after try and catch whether the try completed or threw.
wrongs: A block that runs only when an exception was caught.
A clause on the method header that lists exceptions.
A resource declaration that closes files by itself.
why: Cleanup placed there runs on both the normal path and the exceptional path.
example: A method closes a scanner in this block so the scanner closes even when parsing throws.
scenario: A lock must be released both when the work succeeds and when it throws. Where should the unlock call go?
scenarioWhy: Finally runs after success and after an exception, so the lock is released on both paths.

definition: A try statement that automatically closes AutoCloseable resources declared in its parentheses.
wrongs: A finally block the programmer must write to call close.
A catch that handles only unchecked exceptions.
A synchronized block that locks a file object.
why: Resources declared in the try header are closed when the block ends, including when an exception is thrown.
example: A buffered reader opened in the try header closes when the block finishes, even if readLine throws.
scenario: A file reader must close even if reading throws, and the team does not want a handwritten close call. Which statement does that?
scenarioWhy: Declaring the reader in the try header closes it automatically when the block exits.

definition: The part of a method header that lists checked exceptions the method may pass to its caller.
wrongs: A catch block that handles an exception inside the method.
A finally block that always closes a file.
A generic bound on a type parameter.
why: Declaring the exception forces callers to catch it or declare it themselves.
example: A load method header lists IOException so callers know load may fail while reading.
scenario: A method does not catch IOException and wants its caller to handle that failure. What must the method header include?
scenarioWhy: A throws clause passes the checked IOException to the caller instead of handling it inside the method.

definition: A compact expression that supplies the body of a functional interface without a named class.
wrongs: A named class that implements several unrelated methods.
A package declaration at the top of a file.
A generic wildcard in a parameter type.
why: The compiler turns the expression into an instance of the target interface's single abstract method.
example: A sort call compares names with (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length() instead of a named comparison class.
scenario: A button needs one piece of click behavior, and the team wants to avoid declaring a named class. What should they write?
scenarioWhy: A lambda implements the listener's single method inline, so no named class is required.

definition: An interface with exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can implement it.
wrongs: An interface with several abstract methods and no default methods.
A class that cannot be subclassed.
An annotation that is retained only in source code.
why: The single abstract method gives the lambda exactly one signature to implement.
example: Predicate declares only the abstract method test, so a lambda can act as a Predicate.
scenario: An interface is meant to be implemented by lambdas and declares only one abstract method. What kind of interface is it?
scenarioWhy: One abstract method is what lets the compiler match a lambda to that interface.

definition: A shorthand that refers to an existing method where a lambda would otherwise be written.
wrongs: A throws clause that names a checked exception.
A wildcard import of every type in a package.
A cast from a superclass to a subclass.
why: The referenced method must match the single abstract method of the target functional interface.
example: names.forEach(System.out::println) passes the existing println method instead of a lambda body.
scenario: A stream's forEach should call the existing println method without writing lambda parameters. Which syntax does that?
scenarioWhy: A method reference points at println, and its signature matches the consumer forEach expects.

definition: A pipeline that processes a sequence of elements through intermediate and terminal operations.
wrongs: A resizable array that is always modified in place.
A thread pool that runs one task per element immediately.
A database cursor returned by a query.
why: The pipeline describes work but does not run it until a terminal operation asks for a result.
example: Orders are filtered to the open ones, mapped to totals, and collected, leaving the original list unchanged.
scenario: A list of orders should be filtered and mapped without changing the original list in place. Which API fits?
scenarioWhy: A stream builds a new result from the list instead of rewriting the list's elements.

definition: A lazy stream step, such as filter or map, that returns another stream.
wrongs: A stream step that produces a final value and ends the pipeline.
A terminal collector that builds a concrete list.
A source that creates the stream from a collection.
why: These steps are recorded and run only when a later terminal operation pulls values through the pipeline.
example: Logging inside map prints nothing until a later collect or forEach actually runs the pipeline.
scenario: A pipeline calls filter and map but never a terminating call, and logging inside map never appears. Why did the work not run?
scenarioWrongs: Map runs only on a second thread
scenarioWhy: Filter and map are intermediate, so they do no work until a terminal operation pulls elements.

definition: A stream step that consumes the pipeline and produces a result or a side effect.
wrongs: A lazy step such as filter that returns another stream.
A source method such as stream() on a list.
A collector implementation that is never invoked.
why: Operations such as collect, reduce, and forEach start evaluation, and the stream cannot be reused afterward.
example: Calling collect to build a list forces the earlier filter and map steps to run.
scenario: A pipeline of filter and map should actually run and return a list. What kind of call must finish the pipeline?
scenarioWhy: Only a terminal operation such as collect pulls values through the pipeline and yields the list.

definition: A container that either holds one value or is empty, used instead of returning null.
wrongs: A list that may contain several matching values.
A checked exception thrown when a lookup fails.
A nullable primitive such as int.
why: Callers handle presence with methods such as orElse or ifPresent, so a missing value is explicit.
example: A user lookup returns an empty container when no row matches, and the caller uses orElseThrow.
scenario: A lookup may find no user, and callers should handle absence without testing a null return. What should the method return?
scenarioWhy: Optional makes the missing user explicit, so the caller uses orElse or a similar method instead of a null test.

definition: An independent path of execution that can run alongside other paths in the same process.
wrongs: A separate operating-system process with its own private heap.
A lock that allows only one method to run.
A pool that reuses workers but is not itself a single path of execution.
why: Each thread has its own stack and program counter while sharing the process heap.
example: A server handles a slow report on a worker so the thread that accepts new connections can keep running.
scenario: A download should continue while the user-interface path keeps painting the window. What should run the download?
scenarioWhy: A second thread can run the download while the interface thread continues to paint.

definition: A functional interface whose run method is the code a thread or executor should execute.
wrongs: An interface used to write an object as bytes.
An interface that defines a natural sort order.
An interface for objects that must be closed.
why: Thread and executor APIs accept it and call run on the chosen worker.
example: new Thread(() -> saveReport()).start() runs saveReport as the body of run.
scenario: Work should be handed to a Thread without subclassing Thread. Which type should that work implement?
scenarioWhy: Thread accepts a Runnable and calls its run method, so Thread itself need not be subclassed.

definition: A modifier that lets only one thread at a time execute a method or block on a given lock.
wrongs: A field modifier that only makes writes visible and does not exclude other threads.
A modifier that skips serialization of a field.
A modifier that allows a method to be implemented in native code.
why: The lock is acquired on entry and released on exit, including when the block throws.
example: Two threads calling a locked increment method cannot lose updates to a shared counter.
scenario: Two threads update a shared balance and sometimes lose an increment. Which keyword can make the update method mutually exclusive?
scenarioWhy: synchronized acquires the method's lock so only one thread runs the balance update at a time.

definition: A field whose writes are made visible to other threads and are not freely reordered.
wrongs: A field that only one thread may update because the field itself is a lock.
A field excluded from serialization.
A local variable stored in a method frame.
why: A write to the field happens-before a later read of that field, but a compound action such as increment is still not atomic.
example: A worker loop notices a shutdown flag after another thread sets that flag, without taking a lock.
scenario: A worker loops on a boolean that another thread sets to true, but the worker never notices the write. Which modifier should the field have?
scenarioWhy: volatile makes the write to the flag visible to the worker thread that keeps reading it.

definition: A group of reusable worker threads that execute submitted tasks.
wrongs: A new operating-system process created for every task.
A single thread that must finish before the next task object can be constructed.
A synchronized class with no worker threads.
why: Reusing workers avoids the cost of creating a thread for every short task.
example: A fixed pool of eight workers runs incoming web jobs instead of allocating a new thread per request.
scenario: A server runs thousands of short tasks per minute and should not construct a new Thread for each one. What should execute the tasks?
scenarioWhy: Workers in a pool stay alive and take the next submitted task, avoiding a thread creation per task.

definition: The standard Java API for connecting to relational databases and executing SQL.
wrongs: A library for building graphical windows and buttons.
A protocol for calling methods on objects in another process.
An API for looking up names in a directory service.
why: Drivers implement the same interfaces, so application code can talk to different databases through one API.
example: A program uses DriverManager and Connection from java.sql to query a PostgreSQL database.
scenario: Java code must send SQL to a relational database without tying every call site to one vendor's classes. Which API is the usual choice?
scenarioWhy: JDBC defines the connection and statement interfaces, and a vendor driver supplies the implementation.

definition: A precompiled SQL statement whose data values are bound separately from the SQL text.
wrongs: A statement built by concatenating user input into the SQL string.
A cursor that only walks rows after a query has run.
A pooled connection with no SQL of its own.
why: Placeholders keep values out of the SQL text, which blocks injection and lets the database reuse a plan.
example: A query uses a question-mark placeholder for a user id, then setInt binds the id before execution.
scenario: User input must filter a query and must not be pasted into the SQL string. Which JDBC type should run that query?
scenarioWhy: Binding the input to a placeholder sends it as data, not as part of the SQL text.

definition: An object that represents the rows returned by a JDBC query and lets the code read them.
wrongs: A connection to the database server.
A precompiled statement with unbound placeholders.
A metadata object that describes tables but not this query's rows.
why: next moves the cursor, and getter methods read column values from the current row.
example: After executeQuery, a loop calls next and getString on the email column for each user row.
scenario: A query has already run, and the code must walk each returned row to read column values. Which object does it advance?
scenarioWhy: The result set is the cursor over the query rows, advanced with next and read with column getters.

definition: Converting an object's field values into a byte stream that can later rebuild the object.
wrongs: Writing SQL rows through a database driver.
Compiling a class into bytecode.
Ordering objects with compareTo.
why: A class implements Serializable so an object output stream can write its non-transient fields.
example: A game writes a Player with an object output stream and later reads that stream back into a Player.
scenario: A game must save a Player object's fields to a file and rebuild that object later with JDK object streams. Which mechanism fits?
scenarioWhy: Object streams write a Serializable object's fields and can read those bytes back into an object.
